newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan epidemic sparks pork-to-the-people drive.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan epidemic sparks pork-to-the-people drive.

text.p: Taiwan meatpackers and officials held pork "eat-ins" on Monday in an islandwide campaign to ease public fears over a pig epidemic, handing out free steaks, sweet and sour pork and a Chinese favourite -- stewed pig knuckles.
The knuckles were crucial, after days of graphic television news coverage of the mass slaughter of thousands of swine with the telltale symptoms of foot and mouth disease -- infected hooves.

"Tasty, juicy, you really want to take a bite!" said the slogan under a colour picture of a steaming pig knuckle splashed across top newspapers' front pages in ads bought by hard-hit meatpackers and feed firms.
"When was the last time you savoured a delectable pork knuckle?" said another.

Many Taiwan consumers have not touched pork since March 20, when the cabinet's Council of Agriculture confirmed finding foot and mouth disease and ordered a ban on exports and massive slaughter and vaccination programme.

As of late on Friday, the deadly contagion had been detected on 1,008 of the island's 25,000 farms with officials projecting that 886,000 pigs would have to be destroyed, though only 160,315 had been slaughtered to date.
Farmers and soldiers were slaughtering all hogs -- healthy or otherwise -- at all farms struck by the virus, while all cloven-hoofed livestock were being vaccinated at healthy farms.
Despite the pressing need, Taiwan responded cooly to rival China's offer on Monday to supply vaccines.

Farm council officials questioned the quality of communist China's vaccines and said the Nationalist-ruled island had never issued permits to import them from the mainland. The sides have been political rivals since a civil war split them in 1949.
Taiwan has begun emergency imports of vaccines to inoculate its healthy livestock against hog foot and mouth disease.
Millions of doses were being airlifted in from Britain, France, the United States and other sources whose production met Taiwan's quality requirements.
The crisis has hit farmers and meatpackers hard and since Saturday they have been fighting back, joining with officials to hold festive outdoor eat-ins featuring pork giveaways.
"Healthy pigs are safe to eat," newly elected Taoyuan County magistrate Annette Lu said as she tucked into a knuckle.
State television showed dozens of people happily feasting on free lunch boxes of pig's feet and noodles.
The Consumers' Foundation said people had a right to ask pork sellers for certificates proving their meats were safe and should not fear eating certified pork.
"If sellers provide government-issued certificates, the pork products will be safe," a foundation official said.
Such certificates have been appearing in restaurant windows and grocery meat departments across Taiwan.
Much rides on the success of the massive promotion, as pork prices are 60 percent or more below their pre-epidemic levels.

Pork trading resumed on Saturday at the island's major hog wholesale centres, most of which suspended operations on March 24 in a failed bid to bolster prices. The shutdown gave meatpackers time to launch the drive to restore confidence.
